items.title: Representations and primitive representations as sums of two squares
The Brahmagupta–Fibonacci two-square identity
items.strategy: Expand both displayed pairs of squares and cancel the cross terms. Record both sign variants because later multiplication and primitivity arguments need the freedom to choose either one. The calculation holds for all integer inputs, including zeros.

items.title: Sums of two squares are closed under products
items.strategy: Choose ordered integer representations of the two nonnegative factors and apply either sign variant of the Brahmagupta–Fibonacci identity. If either factor is zero, its only representation is $(0,0)$ and the same formula still gives the zero product.

items.title: Representations of an odd integer correspond to representations of twice that integer
items.strategy: For odd positive $m$, send $(x,y)$ to $(x+y,x-y)$. Expansion gives a representation of $2m$. Conversely a representation $u^2+v^2=2m$ has $u,v$ both odd, so the inverse half-sums are integers. Verify the two composites and prove that the maps preserve coordinate gcd one by reducing any alleged common divisor to a common prime divisor.

items.title: A prime congruent to $3$ modulo $4$ divides both coordinates of a divisible two-square sum
items.strategy: Let $q\equiv3\pmod4$ be prime and suppose $q\mid x^2+y^2$. If one coordinate is divisible by $q$, Euclid's lemma gives divisibility of the other. If neither is, divide by $y^2$ in $\mathbb Z/q$ to make $-1$ a square, contradicting the first supplement. Hence $q\mid x,y$ and therefore $q^2\mid x^2+y^2$.

items.title: Every nonzero residue modulo an odd prime is a sum of two squares
items.strategy: In $\mathbb Z/p$, the set of all square classes, including zero, has $(p+1)/2$ elements. Its translate $a-Q$ has the same size. If the two sets were disjoint, their union would have $p+1$ elements while lying inside the $p$-element quotient. Their intersection therefore supplies $x^2=a-y^2$.

items.title: Thue's lemma on small nonzero representatives
items.strategy: For prime $p$ and $p\nmid a$, let $h$ be the largest natural number with $h^2<p$, obtained from a nonempty finite search below $p$. Primality excludes $(h+1)^2=p$, so $(h+1)^2>p$. Map the $(h+1)^2$ pairs $0\le i,j\le h$ to $ia-j$ modulo $p$ and apply strong pigeonhole. Differences of a colliding pair give $ra\equiv s\pmod p$ with $|r|,|s|\le h<\sqrt p$; the coprimality hypothesis and the strict range force both differences to be nonzero.

items.title: Fermat's two-square theorem for primes
items.strategy: Squares modulo four prove necessity, with $2=1^2+1^2$ handled separately. For an odd prime $p\equiv1\pmod4$, the first supplement gives a square root $a$ of $-1$ modulo $p$. Thue's lemma produces nonzero $r,s$ below $\sqrt p$ with $ra\equiv s$; then $p\mid r^2+s^2$ and $0<r^2+s^2<2p$, so the positive multiple is exactly $p$.

items.title: Two essentially different two-square representations factor an odd integer
items.strategy: Normalize the two positive representations so their first coordinates are odd, their second coordinates are even, and $0<x<u$, which forces $0<v<y$. Factor $(u-x)(u+x)=(y-v)(y+v)$ after dividing all four factors by two. Split the two cross factors by their gcd and use coprime divisibility to obtain positive $e,f,g,h$ with $x+iy=(e+if)(g+ih)$. Taking the elementary norm identity gives $N=(e^2+f^2)(g^2+h^2)$ with both factors greater than one.

items.title: A prime congruent to $1$ modulo $4$ has one two-square representation up to signs and order
items.strategy: Fermat's theorem supplies a representation. For an odd prime the two nonzero coordinates have opposite parity, so normalize every representation to positive coordinates with the odd coordinate first. If two normalized pairs differed, order their odd coordinates and apply the factorisation lemma, contradicting primality. Undoing the normalization shows that every ordered signed representation comes from the unique positive odd-even pair by signs and interchange.

items.title: Prime powers represented as sums of two squares
items.strategy: Treat exponent zero as $1=1^2+0^2$. Powers of $2$ and of primes congruent to one modulo four follow by induction from their prime representations and product closure. For $q\equiv3\pmod4$, even powers have the explicit representation $(q^j)^2+0^2$; if an odd power were represented, repeatedly divide both coordinates by $q$ using the three-mod-four divisibility lemma until an impossible representation of $q$ remained.

items.title: Characterisation of positive integers that are sums of two squares
items.strategy: Use canonical prime factorisation. If every prime congruent to three modulo four has even valuation, represent each prime-power factor by the preceding lemma and multiply the finite list. Conversely, for a represented integer and such a prime $q$, the local divisibility lemma removes $q^2$ from the integer and $q$ from both coordinates. Induction on $v_q(n)$ excludes a final odd exponent and proves that every such valuation is even. Include $n=1$ through the empty factorisation.

items.title: Coprime primitively represented factors have a primitive product representation
items.strategy: Let $P=a^2+b^2$ and $Q=c^2+d^2$ be primitive with $\gcd(P,Q)=1$, and use $(ac-bd,ad+bc)$ for the product. If a prime divided both new coordinates, the two linear combinations with $a,b$ would force it to divide $P$, while the two combinations with $c,d$ would force it to divide $Q$; primitivity rules out the alternative in each case. This contradicts coprimality of $P,Q$.

items.title: Powers of primes congruent to $1$ modulo $4$ have primitive two-square representations
items.strategy: Induct from $(1,0)$ and a primitive representation $p=a^2+b^2$. Given a primitive representation $(u,v)$ of $p^e$, the two sign variants of the identity give candidate representations of $p^{e+1}$. Any prime common to a candidate's coordinates must be $p$. If both candidates had both coordinates divisible by $p$, their sums and differences would force $p\mid u,v$, since $p$ is odd and divides neither $a$ nor $b$. Thus at least one candidate is primitive.

items.title: Characterisation of primitive sums of two squares
items.strategy: If $n=x^2+y^2$ with $\gcd(x,y)=1$, the three-mod-four divisibility lemma excludes every prime congruent to three modulo four, and reduction modulo four shows that $4\nmid n$, equivalently $v_2(n)\le1$. Conversely factor $n$ into a possible single factor $2$ and powers of distinct primes congruent to one modulo four. Represent those prime powers primitively and combine the pairwise-coprime factors using the primitive-product lemma, with the empty factorisation giving $n=1$.

items.title: Primitive sums of two squares are closed under products unless both factors are even
items.strategy: Apply the primitive characterisation to the two positive factors. Neither has a prime divisor congruent to three modulo four. Each has $2$-valuation at most one, and the condition that they are not both even makes the sum of their $2$-valuations at most one. Valuation additivity and the characterisation then give a primitive representation of the product.

items.title: Divisors greater than one of primitively represented integers are primitively represented
items.strategy: Let $d>1$ divide a positive integer $n$ with a primitive two-square representation. Every prime exponent of $d$ is at most the corresponding exponent of $n$. Hence $d$ has no prime divisor congruent to three modulo four and has $2$-valuation at most one. Apply the primitive characterisation.

items.title: Squarefree sums of two squares
items.strategy: For squarefree positive $n$, every prime valuation is zero or one, so the general criterion reduces to the absence of odd prime factors congruent to three modulo four. If a representation had coordinate gcd greater than one, a prime dividing that gcd would have its square divide $n$, contradicting squarefreeness. Thus every representation of an eligible squarefree integer is primitive, including the empty-factor case $n=1$.

items.title: Thue's collision argument gives $73=3^2+8^2$
items.strategy: Verify $27^2\equiv-1\pmod{73}$ and take $h=8$. The pairs $(0,0)$ and $(3,8)$ collide under $(i,j)\mapsto27i-j\pmod{73}$, so the difference gives $3\cdot27\equiv8$. Multiplying the root congruence gives $73\mid3^2+8^2$, while the small bounds force equality.

items.title: Extended Euclid gives $73=3^2+8^2$ from the root $27$ of $-1$
items.strategy: Verify $27^2\equiv-1\pmod{73}$ and run $73=2\cdot27+19$, $27=19+8$. Back-substitution gives $8=3\cdot27-73$, hence $3\cdot27\equiv8\pmod{73}$. Squaring and using the root congruence shows $73\mid3^2+8^2$, and direct evaluation gives equality. This is the source's Euclidean route, distinct from the preceding collision route.

items.title: Prime factorisation gives two representations of $221$ as a sum of two squares
items.strategy: Use $13=2^2+3^2$ and $17=1^2+4^2$. The two sign variants of the identity give $221=10^2+11^2=14^2+5^2$. Verify both equalities directly and record that composite integers need not inherit prime uniqueness.

items.title: $539=7^2\cdot11$ is not a sum of two squares
items.strategy: Refute the claim that every positive integer is a sum of two squares. If $539=x^2+y^2$, the prime $11\equiv3\pmod4$ would divide both coordinates, so $11^2$ would divide $539$. Its displayed prime factorisation has $11$ to exponent one, a contradiction. Relate this direct obstruction to the general valuation criterion.

items.title: The representations $221=5^2+14^2=11^2+10^2$ recover the factors $13$ and $17$
items.strategy: Normalize the two representations with odd coordinates first and apply the factorisation construction. The half-sums and half-differences yield $e=2,f=3,g=4,h=1$, so the two proper factors are $e^2+f^2=13$ and $g^2+h^2=17$. Check their product and both original representations.

items.title: The primitive two-square criterion distinguishes $289$, $34$, and $833$
items.strategy: Verify the primitive representations $289=15^2+8^2$ and $34=3^2+5^2$. Verify $833=28^2+7^2$, but note that $7\equiv3\pmod4$ divides $833$, so the primitive criterion forbids every primitive representation even though a nonprimitive one exists. Check the displayed coordinate gcds and prime factors.

items.title: $68=8^2+2^2$ is representable but has no primitive two-square representation
items.strategy: Refute the claim that every represented positive integer is primitively represented. Squares modulo four are zero or one, so a representation of a multiple of four must have both coordinates even. Apply this to $68=8^2+2^2$ and compare with the $2$-valuation clause of the primitive criterion.

items.title: Squarefree sums of two squares up to $30$
items.strategy: List the squarefree positive integers at most $30$, discard exactly those with an odd prime factor congruent to three modulo four, and obtain $1,2,5,10,13,17,26,29$. Give an explicit two-square representation of each retained integer and verify that every coordinate gcd is one. This is a bounded, independently checkable construction.

title: Frattini Subgroups and the Burnside Basis Theorem

items.title: The Frattini subgroup of a finite group is characteristic
items.strategy: Every automorphism sends maximal proper subgroups to maximal proper subgroups, hence permutes the family whose intersection is $\Phi(G)$. Taking the image of that intersection gives the same intersection. Treat the trivial group through the published empty-intersection convention.

items.title: Generation of a finite group is detected modulo its Frattini subgroup
items.strategy: The forward implication follows by applying the quotient map. Conversely, generation of the quotient gives $G=\langle S\rangle\Phi(G)$. Since $G$ is finite, list the finitely many elements of $\Phi(G)$ adjoined to $S$ and remove them one at a time using the nongenerator characterization. The trivial group and $S=\varnothing$ are included.

items.title: Elementary abelian $p$-groups
An elementary abelian $p$-group has a canonical $\mathbb F_p$-vector-space structure
items.strategy: For $\bar a\in\mathbb Z/p$ and $x\in E$, define $\bar a\cdot x=x^a$. Exponent $p$ makes this independent of the representative, commutativity converts addition of scalars into multiplication in $E$, and the group power laws verify the remaining scalar axioms. Conversely the additive group of any finite $\mathbb F_p$-linear structure is elementary abelian. State the zero group and the scalars $0,1$ explicitly.

items.title: $\mathbb F_p$-spanning sets, independence, and bases in an elementary abelian $p$-group
Finite elementary abelian $p$-groups have bases, basis extension, and a well-defined dimension
items.strategy: Starting from a finite spanning set, delete redundant elements until a basis remains; starting from an independent set, adjoin elements outside its span until it spans. For any basis $B$, unique coordinates give a bijection $(\mathbb Z/p)^B\to E$, so $|E|=p^{|B|}$ and unique prime factorization makes all basis sizes equal. The empty basis handles $E=1$ without a choice principle.

items.title: The $p$th-power subgroup $G^p$
The Frattini quotient is the largest elementary abelian quotient of a finite $p$-group
items.strategy: Every maximal subgroup of the finite $p$-group is normal of index $p$, so every commutator and every $p$th power lies in their intersection; hence $P/\Phi(P)$ is elementary abelian. If $N\trianglelefteq P$ and $P/N$ is elementary abelian, extend each nonzero coset to a finite basis, omit that basis vector to obtain a maximal subgroup of $P/N$, and pull it back. The intersection of these pullbacks is $N$, so $\Phi(P)\le N$. Include $P=1$, $N=P$, and both directions of the equivalence.

items.title: $\Phi(P)=P'P^p$ for a finite $p$-group
items.strategy: First show that $P^p$ is characteristic and hence normal; $P'$ is normal, so $P'P^p$ is a normal subgroup. The elementary-abelian Frattini quotient kills commutators and $p$th powers, giving $P'P^p\le\Phi(P)$. Conversely $P/P'P^p$ is abelian of exponent $p$, so the largest-elementary-abelian-quotient theorem gives $\Phi(P)\le P'P^p$. Check the trivial group and $p=2$.

items.title: If $H\le P$ are finite $p$-groups, then $\Phi(H)\le\Phi(P)$
items.strategy: Apply the Frattini formula to both groups. Every commutator of elements of $H$ is a commutator in $P$, and every $p$th power from $H$ is a $p$th power from $P$, so $H'H^p\le P'P^p$. Include $H=1$ and $H=P$.

items.title: $\Phi(P/N)=\Phi(P)N/N$ for a normal subgroup of a finite $p$-group
items.strategy: Under the quotient map, commutators map onto $(P/N)'$ and $p$th powers map onto $(P/N)^p$. Apply the Frattini formula on both sides and the quotient group laws to obtain $(P/N)'(P/N)^p=P'P^pN/N$. Check $N=1$, $N=P$, and equality in both inclusions.

items.title: $\Phi(P\times Q)=\Phi(P)\times\Phi(Q)$ for finite $p$-groups
items.strategy: Compute commutators and $p$th powers componentwise in the external direct product: $(P\times Q)'=P'\times Q'$ and $(P\times Q)^p=P^p\times Q^p$. The Frattini formula then gives the equality. Include a trivial factor and the product of two trivial groups.

items.title: $\Phi(P)=P^2$ for a finite $2$-group
items.strategy: The quotient $P/P^2$ has exponent at most two, and every group of exponent two is abelian by expanding $(xy)^2=1$. Hence $P'\le P^2$, and the Frattini formula reduces to $\Phi(P)=P'P^2=P^2$. The trivial group is included.

items.title: A finite $p$-group has trivial Frattini subgroup exactly when it is elementary abelian
items.strategy: If $\Phi(P)=1$, the Frattini quotient theorem identifies $P$ itself as elementary abelian. Conversely, if $P$ is elementary abelian, the quotient by $1$ is elementary abelian, so the minimal-kernel clause gives $\Phi(P)\le1$. Treat $P=1$ and both directions explicitly.

items.title: Minimal generating sets of a group
The generator rank $d(P)$ of a finite $p$-group
Burnside Basis Theorem
items.strategy: Generation of $P$ is equivalent to spanning $P/\Phi(P)$ by the generation-detection corollary. An inclusion-minimal generating set has distinct quotient images and maps bijectively to an inclusion-minimal spanning set, hence to a basis. Conversely, if the quotient map restricts to a bijection from $X$ onto a basis, then $X$ generates and removing any member destroys spanning and therefore generation. State this restricted-bijection clause explicitly so two distinct lifts of one basis vector are not misclassified. Handle $P=1$ with the empty basis.

items.title: Minimal generating sets of a finite $p$-group have size $d(P)$
items.strategy: Burnside basis sends every minimal generating set to a basis, whose size is $d(P)$. Given any generating set, its image spans the Frattini quotient; delete redundant images until a basis remains and lift the corresponding subset. The empty generating set for the trivial group gives size zero.

items.title: Every element outside $\Phi(P)$ belongs to a minimal generating set of $P$
items.strategy: The image of $x\notin\Phi(P)$ is nonzero and hence is a one-element independent set in the Frattini quotient. Extend it to a finite basis without choice, lift the other basis vectors, and apply Burnside basis. Explain why the statement is vacuous for $P=1$.

items.title: A nontrivial finite $p$-group is cyclic exactly when $d(P)=1$
items.strategy: If $d(P)=1$, lift a one-element basis and use Burnside basis to obtain one generator. Conversely, a generator maps to a spanning singleton, so the nonzero Frattini quotient has basis size one. Nontriviality excludes the zero-dimensional quotient; record separately that $d(1)=0$.

items.title: Maximal subgroups of a finite $p$-group are the inverse images of Frattini hyperplanes
items.strategy: Correspondence sends each maximal subgroup $M$ to a maximal proper subgroup of the finite elementary abelian group $P/\Phi(P)$. Extend a basis of that subgroup by one vector to see that it has codimension one and is the kernel of the coordinate homomorphism to $\mathbb Z/p$; conversely the kernel of any nonzero linear homomorphism is a hyperplane whose inverse image is maximal. Treat $P=1$ and the one-dimensional quotient.

items.title: Automorphisms act linearly on the Frattini quotient
items.strategy: Characteristicity of $\Phi(P)$ lets each automorphism of $P$ induce an automorphism of $P/\Phi(P)$. The identity $\alpha(x^a)=\alpha(x)^a$ makes the induced map preserve the canonical $\mathbb F_p$-scalar action. Verify that composition is preserved, obtaining a homomorphism $\rho_P$ from $\operatorname{Aut}(P)$ to the group of $\mathbb F_p$-linear automorphisms of the quotient, including $P=1$.

items.title: Hall–Burnside: coprime automorphisms are detected on the Frattini quotient
items.strategy: Assume a nontrivial $p'$-subgroup $A\le\operatorname{Aut}(P)$ acts trivially on $P/\Phi(P)$. Cauchy's theorem gives an element $\alpha$ of prime order $q\ne p$. It preserves every Frattini coset; the cyclic $q$-group acts on each coset, whose $p$-power size is not divisible by $q$, so each coset has an $\alpha$-fixed representative. Choose fixed representatives of a basis of the quotient, apply Burnside basis, and conclude that $\alpha$ fixes a generating set and is the identity, a contradiction. Include $P=1$ and $A=1$.

items.title: The kernel of the automorphism action on $P/\Phi(P)$ is a $p$-group
items.strategy: The kernel is finite because it is a subgroup of the permutations of finite $P$. If a prime $q\ne p$ divided its order, Cauchy's theorem would produce an order-$q$ subgroup acting trivially on the Frattini quotient, contradicting Hall–Burnside. Unique prime factorization therefore makes the kernel order a power of $p$. Include the trivial kernel and $P=1$.

title: Frattini Subgroups and the Burnside Basis Theorem — Examples

items.title: The Frattini subgroup of a nontrivial cyclic $p$-group
items.strategy: For $P=\langle g\rangle$ of order $p^n$ with $n\ge1$, use the cyclic power-order formula to identify $P^p=\langle g^p\rangle$ and use commutativity to set $P'=1$. The Frattini formula gives $\Phi(P)=\langle g^p\rangle$, the quotient has order $p$, and its one-element basis gives $d(P)=1$. Check $n=1$ separately.

items.title: The Frattini subgroup of $(\mathbb Z/p)^n$ is trivial
items.strategy: With componentwise addition, $(\mathbb Z/p)^n$ is elementary abelian, including the empty product at $n=0$. The Frattini-free characterization gives $\Phi((\mathbb Z/p)^n)=1$. The coordinate vectors form a basis in the native finite $\mathbb F_p$ sense, so the generator rank is $n$.

items.title: The Frattini subgroups of $D_8$ and $Q_8$
items.strategy: Use the semidirect-product normal forms for $D_8=\operatorname{Dih}(C_4)$ to compute $D_8'=D_8^2=\langle r^2\rangle$. In $Q_8$, the quaternion multiplication table gives $Q_8'=Q_8^2=\{\pm1\}$. The finite-two-group formula yields both Frattini subgroups; in each case the quotient is $(\mathbb Z/2)^2$ and the generator rank is two.

items.title: The $3\times3$ upper-unitriangular groups have generator rank two
items.strategy: For each prime $p$, construct $H_p=(\mathbb Z/p)^3$ with $(a,b,c)(a',b',c')=(a+a',b+b',c+c'+ab')$ and verify associativity, identity, inverses, and order $p^3$. Direct commutator calculation gives $H_p'=\{(0,0,c)\}$; for odd $p$ all $p$th powers are trivial, while for $p=2$ every square lies on the same central axis. The Frattini formula therefore gives $\Phi(H_p)=\{(0,0,c)\}$, and the first two coordinate classes form a basis of the quotient. This includes $p=2$ without assuming exponent $p$.

items.title: The maximal subgroups of $D_8$ as Frattini hyperplanes
items.strategy: For $D_8=\langle r,s\rangle$ from the preceding example, list the three maximal subgroups $\langle r\rangle$, $\langle r^2,s\rangle$, and $\langle r^2,rs\rangle$. Modulo $\Phi(D_8)=\langle r^2\rangle$, identify them with the three one-dimensional subgroups of $(\mathbb Z/2)^2$ and write the three nonzero coordinate-sum homomorphisms whose kernels they are.

items.title: A nonsurjective homomorphism need not carry the Frattini subgroup into the target Frattini subgroup
items.strategy: Embed $C_4=\langle g\rangle$ in $S_5$ by sending $g$ to $(1\,2\,3\,4)$. The cyclic example gives $\Phi(C_4)=\langle g^2\rangle$, whose image contains the nonidentity double transposition $(1\,3)(2\,4)$. The Frattini subgroup of $S_5$ is nilpotent and normal; the normal-subgroup classification leaves $1,A_5,S_5$, and the latter two are not solvable and hence not nilpotent, so $\Phi(S_5)=1$. Thus the image inclusion fails, while surjectivity remains the exact valid hypothesis.

items.title: The Fitting subgroup of $A_5$ does not contain its centralizer
items.strategy: The Fitting subgroup is normal and nilpotent. Simplicity of $A_5$ makes it either $1$ or $A_5$; the second option would make $A_5$ nilpotent and therefore solvable, contradicting the published nonsolvability theorem. Hence $F(A_5)=1$, so $C_{A_5}(F(A_5))=A_5\nleq1$. This isolates the solvability hypothesis in the published self-centralization theorem.

items.title: Inversion on $C_3$ is detected on its Frattini quotient
items.strategy: The cyclic example gives $\Phi(C_3)=1$. Inversion is a nonidentity automorphism of order two, coprime to three, and its induced action on $C_3/\Phi(C_3)=C_3$ is still inversion. This concrete action illustrates the Hall–Burnside conclusion and checks that the theorem does not claim such automorphisms are absent, only that their quotient action is faithful.

items.title: FALSE: the Frattini subgroup is the union of the maximal subgroups
items.strategy: In $(\mathbb Z/2)^2$, the Frattini subgroup is trivial, while every nonzero vector spans one of the three maximal order-two subgroups. Their union is the whole four-element group. Thus union and intersection differ maximally in this example.

items.title: FALSE: every homomorphism carries the Frattini subgroup into the target Frattini subgroup
items.strategy: Invoke the preceding explicit embedding $C_4\hookrightarrow S_5$: its image of $\Phi(C_4)$ is nontrivial while $\Phi(S_5)=1$. State the valid surjective-image inclusion separately and identify nonsurjectivity as the missing hypothesis.

items.title: FALSE: all minimal generating sets of a finite group have the same size
items.strategy: In the additive cyclic group $\mathbb Z/6$, the singleton $\{1\}$ is a minimal generating set, while $\{2,3\}$ also generates and neither singleton does. Hence the two inclusion-minimal generating sets have different sizes; the finite-$p$ hypothesis in Burnside basis cannot be removed.

items.title: FALSE: the Fitting subgroup always contains its centralizer
items.strategy: Use the preceding $A_5$ computation: $F(A_5)=1$ and $C_{A_5}(F(A_5))=A_5$. Contrast it with the published theorem for finite solvable groups, identifying solvability as the missing hypothesis.
